title: The emperor's notebook
hook: Marcus wrote in Greek, to himself, often on campaign, and the title "Meditations" came later

segments.voice: Yesterday, the week closed with Rumi as he was: a Muslim, a scholar, a Sufi. Your line was keep him whole. Did you meet a quote that was missing something? Day one hundred sixty-four.

Imagine someone found your notes app. Not your posts, your notes. The reminders to yourself. Be patient with Dad. Stop checking your phone. You're not as tired as you think. It would be a little embarrassing, and also the truest picture of you anyone could get. Now picture a tent on a cold riverbank in central Europe, around the year 170. Outside, the Roman army. Inside, by lamplight, the most powerful man in the world, writing notes to himself about how to be a decent person. He never meant anyone to read them. Today, the emperor's notebook.
screen: `YOUR NOTES APP, NOT YOUR POSTS.` → `A TENT ON THE DANUBE, AROUND 170.` → `THE EMPEROR'S NOTEBOOK.`

segments.voice: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome from 161 to 180. He spent much of his last decade at war along the Danube frontier, and it's likely that much of his notebook was written there, in camp. A few section headings survive in the manuscripts that seem to place him: one book ends with a note that it was written among the Quadi, a people on the far side of the river, and another begins, this at Carnuntum, a Roman fort. Three things are worth knowing. First, he wrote in Greek, not Latin. Greek was the language of philosophy, and Marcus had studied the Stoics, especially the teachings of the former slave Epictetus, since his youth. Second, he wrote to himself. The notes scold, remind, encourage, and repeat. He tells himself the same things again and again, the way you do when you haven't learned them yet. That's part of why they feel so alive: this isn't a man who has arrived, it's a man practicing. Third, the famous title isn't his. The old manuscripts carry a Greek heading usually translated to himself, and it may have been added by whoever copied the notes after his death. Meditations is what English readers later called the book. It survived by a thin thread of copies and was first printed in the 1550s. So when we read Marcus beside Rumi this camp, remember the difference. Rumi spoke his book aloud to a friend who wrote it down. Marcus wrote his alone, for no one. Both, somehow, reached us.
screen: `WRITTEN ON CAMPAIGN, BY THE DANUBE.` · `IN GREEK, THE LANGUAGE OF PHILOSOPHY.` · `NOTES THAT SCOLD AND REPEAT.` · `THE TITLE CAME LATER.` · then, large: `TO HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one note to yourself. Settle, and breathe. Ask what you keep needing to remember and keep forgetting. Be kinder to your sister. Rest is not failure. Finish before you start the next thing. Find one sentence, plain and honest, the way you'd say it to a friend. Say it inside, slowly. Then, if you can, write it down somewhere you'll see it again. The bell holds the time.
The emperor's notebook. Marcus Aurelius's private notes, written in Greek, often on campaign, headed to himself; we call them the Meditations. Today's word.
Your line: to himself. Today, read your note to yourself once in the afternoon and once at night, the way Marcus reread his. Day one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Readers of the Meditations often keep it by the bed and read a single short section at a time, and many who follow modern Stoic practice keep their own journal of notes to themselves.

notes: Headings: book 1 ends 'among the Quadi at the Granua'; book 2 begins 'at Carnuntum'. Whether these are Marcus's own is debated. Confirm.
First printed edition: Xylander, Zurich, 1558/1559; script says 'the 1550s'. Confirm.
The Greek title ta eis heauton may be a later addition; stated with 'may'. Confirm.
Epictetus's influence (via the Discourses, which Marcus says Rusticus lent him, Meditations 1.7): confirm 'since his youth' is not overstated.
Dating: much written in the 170s; 'around the year 170' used for the scene. Confirm.
